title: Cut or Hold
passages:
The seaward gap went first.

The squall's leading edge came through it low and flat, the way water moves when it has somewhere to be, and it got under the ward door and threw it back on its hinge. The door was a slab of green steel as tall as a market stall, hung wrong for fourteen years, and the wind took it all the way until the hinge let go with a sound like a cable parting. It stopped against the far wall. The floor jumped. Wren felt it come up through her boots into her knees.

The Caller's timer arm jumped with it.

That brass finger measured slack water — it was the thing that said *now, the tide has stopped, pay the bell now and no other minute* — and Wren had seated it in its notch herself, with her own thumb, an hour ago. The shock knocked it clean out. The hammer lifted. The governor that should have held it back had been dead since the medicine drawer turned green. So the Caller rang.

No one was within a meter of it. Mara's hands were up on the rope and the rope was slack. Dey was against the wall with Wren's palm still mashed over his mouth. Nia had both fists on the cold-case lid. And the big bell rang anyway, one note with a floor under it that Wren felt in her back teeth, and out of it came a voice off the copper line.

Bayo's voice. Warm. Easy. Sure of itself the way he always was.

*I've got the line. I'm holding. I'm not going anywhere.*

Dey made a noise behind Wren's hand. She didn't let him up.

She had the slate out before the note finished dying. The corner of the screen still sat amber. She woke it with her thumb and pulled the queue — the roll of voices the Caller kept stacked in that thick, cold ward air, every one of them waiting its turn to be handed back at slack water. Her eleven seconds had headed that roll an hour ago. She'd put them there herself, palm flat on the brass, and whatever reason she'd had for keeping them was gone out of her now, wiped so clean she couldn't have said what they'd been about if you paid her. The entry sat there in her own hand. *11 sec. Front. Served.*

The queue had moved.

Something had gone out in front of it. Bayo's voice was at the top of the roll now, warm and certain and about to turn into a lie, and the arm had not been touched and the tide was not slack — the water was already leaning seaward, sucking at the gap, dragging the whole tower a hair with every pull. The Caller was paying out on its own, like a till that had lost the trick of stopping.

She understood the rest a half-second later, and it went through her colder than the water would have. The copper had been open the whole time. Everything anyone said topside, anywhere near that line on the *Marrow*, was running down into the bell and stacking up in the queue. And the bell did not hand a voice back for free. It kept it, and it took the piece of the speaker that made it.

Bayo had just paid in without knowing.

*Queue advanced. No hand. No slack,* Wren typed, and her thumb was not quite steady. She put that in the margin too, the way she'd learned to put everything in the margin, because the one time she hadn't was the reason she was standing in a dead ward with a hollowed woman asking, pleasant as weather, over her shoulder:

"Who's first, then?"

Wren didn't answer her. Answering was how you got on the roll, and she had already put eleven seconds of herself in this room tonight. She wasn't putting her instructions in too.

The ascent line lay in a coil by the lift-frame, the rope that would take them up the shaft to the *Marrow*'s drum, soft three-strand, marked every fathom with a whipping of twine so a diver could feel in the dark how much he had left. It ran out the door and up into the dark, and the water on the floor grating was going after it, thin as a coin, dragging at her boot soles. Seaward. Everything in here leaned seaward now.

The bell rope was in Mara's fists, high up, slack.

Wren took it lower down, hand over hand, the way you'd strip a wet sheet off a line, and Mara opened her fingers. No fight in her at all. She let the rope go the way she must have let everything go for fourteen months, easy, like passing a cup across a table to somebody who hadn't asked.

Wren pulled a bight off the coil, an arm's length and a hand more, and put it in Mara's fists and closed the fingers over it for her.

"It wants hauling," she said. Short. Flat. Dull as a brick. "Arm over arm. Fists to the mark, let it run, take the next."

Mara looked at the line as if somebody had handed her a tool she'd used before and couldn't name. "Does it want it fast?"

"Slow's better."

She set her feet and hauled. Steady. Arm over arm, no slack in her, the coil at her boots growing, wet line stacking wet line. Whatever the deep had eaten out of her had left her hands alone. Her palms were old callus in ridges, cracked at the base of every finger, a crank's year written into skin — and the hands knew the job without waiting on the rest of her.

"Who's first, then," she said, pleasant as weather, to nobody.

Dey came off the wall with his chin up, which was how he answered most things. Wren put the back of her hand on his chest without looking at him. He had a way of volunteering that made you want to find the exits.

The copper came into the ward through a gland in the wall at knee height, and her own tape was still on it, from an hour ago, when she'd been a person who taped things. Behind her the timer arm sat in a notch it had been knocked out of, and the governor that should have held it was dead, so nothing in the world was holding the hammer back but a hole in a piece of brass.

It would ring again. Soon. And Bayo was at the front of the roll with his warm certain voice, and behind him there was a whole topside of people who'd been talking near an open line all night.

Wren counted instead of talking. Twelve arm-lengths in, by the twine marks. Twelve was better than she'd have given a woman that hollow. She had her slate out to write it down when the coil stopped growing.

Mara had stopped. She was still holding the line, both fists, no strain in her, but she'd stopped, and she was looking at Nia.

Nia hadn't moved off the cold-case lid the whole time. She stood with both fists flat on it, suit dripping, fourteen years old, her face doing nothing at all, which Wren had learned tonight was what her face did when it was doing the most.

Mara's eyes went over it slowly. Cheek, brow, mouth, the way you read a gauge you don't trust.

"Whose girl are you?" she said.

Nia didn't answer her. Wren watched her decide not to, the way you hear a hatch come dogged shut and know better than to argue with it.

She came off the cold-case lid and went around behind it to the rack, the bank of drawers, and her hand found the yellow one without her eyes having to. Thumb on the latch. It gave with a dry click, like a knuckle.

The cold came out.

It came out low, the way cold does, off the open drawer and over the grating and across all their boots at once. Fourteen months of it, hoarded and never once let out, because letting it out meant the medicine went warm, and warm meant turned, and turned meant Teo alone with nothing. Wren felt it climb her ankles and take her breath halfway. Dey's breath went white. Mara's went white, and Mara hauled her line straight through the middle of it, arm over arm, and felt nothing at all.

Nia had her suit open at the ribs already. She lifted the wand out of the drawer — glass, no fatter than a finger, the green long gone out of it, the yellow going now, going while Wren stood there and watched, on its way to the red that meant no good to anybody. She pushed it into the flat pocket sewn against her skin and pressed the suit down over it with the heel of her hand.

"Body-warm holds it," she said. To the drawer, not to anyone. "Long as it's body-warm, it holds."

"That's the lot?" Wren said. "That's all of it?"

"Third shelf," Nia said.

And behind her, twelve arm-lengths of wet line stacked at her boots, Mara said it in the same breath.

"Third shelf."

Same two words, same moment, and neither of them turned to look at the other. That went up Wren's back colder than the drawer had.

Nia crossed to the third shelf. Folded steel at chest height, and bare — no drawer, no color, no latch, not even the pale shadow a drawer leaves behind on paint. Steel, and a tidemark of grime where fourteen years of the cold-box had sweated and dried and sweated again.

She put her hand flat on the nothing where the drawer should have been.

"It's empty," she said. Flat as the rest of her. "There's no more. This is it."

Mara hauled. Her eyes had gone off somewhere warm and far away.

"Always the third shelf," she said, helpful as a hand at your elbow, a woman telling strangers where the aspirin lives. "Keep it cranked cold or it turns on you. Cold or it turns. Can't do a thing with it once it's turned."

"Nia," Wren said.

Nia didn't take her hand off the steel. Through the wet of the suit Wren could see the shape of the wand against her ribs, one shade nearer the red than it had been a minute ago.

"Then I hold it," Nia said. Not to Mara. To the shelf. "It's on me now. Nobody cranks anything. I hold it warm and it holds."

She pressed the suit flat over the pocket and left her hand there, and Wren wrote it in the margin of the slate with a thumb that had steadied: *cold-box dead. shelf three bare. all of it on the girl.* Which meant the drawer was out of it now. The dead dynamo couldn't spoil what wasn't in the box, and there was no next dose to lose, and the whole of Teo's medicine was zipped against a fourteen-year-old's ribs where the cold couldn't get at it and neither could the tower.

Behind her the timer arm slid a tooth further along a notch nothing had touched, and the hammer came up again.

The hammer sat at the top of its lift and did not come down, which Wren liked less than if it had. A thing that hasn't fallen can still pick its minute.

The lift-frame was bolted to the grating by the shaft: a hoop of pipe for a back, two planks for a seat, a footboard worn shiny, and a hand-crank on the left side, because a boat that loses its drum up top still has to get a diver out of a hole. Wren had used that crank twice. She had never once thought of it as a problem.

"Up," she said. "Sit down, hold the hoop, don't stand up in it."

Mara sat. She put her hands on the hoop, then took them off it and reached down and found the crank handle by touch, without looking, the way your hand finds a light switch in your own house.

"Is this mine to turn?"

"No." Wren took the soft line off her shoulder — three-strand, no wire in it anywhere, because wire takes a hand off at the knuckle and there was nothing in this tower that could put one back — and made two loops and a hitch around Mara's wrists, snug, not cruel, lashing them to the hoop at the height of her collarbone. Mara watched her do it with polite interest, the way you watch a stranger fold a sheet.

"There's always a crank," she said.

"Not tonight." Wren tested the hitch with her thumb. "Tonight it's a chair with no handle and a woman who sits in it."

"You're sure."

"I'm the topside tech. I'm sure."

Dey already had the tail of the ascent line over his shoulder and his boots on the rungs. The shaft went up out of the ward's roof in a square of green steel, runged, and the water in the bottom eight feet of it was breathing with the ebb, in and out, in and out, sucking at his heels.

"You're hollowed," Wren said.

"I'm hollowed and I've got hands." He was up three rungs before she could get a fist on his ankle, and she didn't, because holding him down would have cost a minute she didn't have. "Somebody's got to lean the drum, and it isn't the girl with the medicine, and it isn't you, because you're cutting copper."

He went up. The line went with him, and the coil on the grating shrank, and Wren stood with the bolt-cutters out of her bag — short ones, the pair she used for slates that had frozen shut — and put her boot on the bottom rung.

The copper ran up the shaft wall in lead clips, a finger's thickness of it, and it ran all the way to the *Marrow*, and it had been running both ways all night: every word anyone said on that boat going down into the ward air and stacking in the bell's queue, Bayo's warm certain voice at the front of the roll, and behind him the whole topside, Sol and Quill's channel and whoever else had opened their mouth near that gland. A tap left on. Cut it and the tap was off. Cut it and she also had no voice to the boat, none, not one word, because there was no other line off this tower.

She climbed six rungs, found the copper, set the cutters, and cut it.

She folded the two ends back on themselves and taped each one to the wall a hand's width apart, so they couldn't touch, because copper that touches is copper that's open. Then she put her mouth to the shaft and shouted up it, "DRUM'S YOURS, TAKE HER SLOW," and the shaft took her voice up the way a chimney takes smoke, thin and all at once.

The drum took the weight. The ascent line came off the grating in one long hiss and went bar-tight, and the frame groaned at its bolts, and Mara came up off the seat a hand's width and hung there with the water sheeting off her boots, fists lashed at her collarbone, hair flat to her skull.

"Are we nearly there?" she asked, pleasant as weather.

"Twelve fathom," Wren said. "Count the twine marks with your heels. Don't talk; talking goes in the bell."

"Does it."

"It does now."

Mara counted with her heels. Wren put her slate up and marked the fathom, and the timer arm slid its last tooth, and outside, past the door that was no longer on its hinge, something heavy hit the water.

Weather slaps. Weather hisses and throws spray and moves on. This arrived. One flat boom with a hull behind it, and the whole tower took the sound through the grating and up into Wren's knees, and then the water came back off it in a long suck, the way it does when something big and floating has just put its shoulder where the shoulder doesn't go.

The barge came in on the squall's back and made no noise doing it.

That was the part Wren's body kept refusing. Everything else on this coast announced itself — the *Marrow*'s two-pot diesel knocked like somebody at a door, the drum screamed when it took weight, Quill's channel hissed all night long — and this came across the water quiet as a hand laid flat on a table. Forty feet of deck plate. No wheelhouse worth the name. No lamp and no mast to hang one on. Riding low at the nose, low enough that the ebb was already coming over the port side in a white sheet.

She was six rungs up the shaft with the water breathing at her shins, and she watched it arrive as a change in the weather: the square of gray above her that had been sky and rain went to black steel, edge to edge.

Then it put its port shoulder into the *Marrow*'s quarter.

The tower took the blow up through the rungs into the arches of her feet. Above her the whole boat came off her fenders and landed again, a sound like a crate dropped off a shoulder, and the ascent line stopped humming.

It went bar-tight. Then it went past that. Below her the lift-frame came up off the grating a hand's width and hung there, and one of the bolts holding it walked out of its hole with a squeal — one thread, two.

Mara's heels came off the footboard.

"That isn't twelve," she said, pleasant as weather.

"Count from where you are."

"Fourteen."

"Then it's fourteen."

Through the hatch Wren had a slice of the deck: Dey with his back into the drum's brake lever and his heels skidding out from under him, and Bayo at the wheel with both hands on it and the wheel over hard and doing nothing whatsoever, because a boat made fast to a tower and a barge in a squall does not steer. It leans.

Rusk came over the rail with a boat hook.

He didn't climb so much as arrive — hook over the rail, ash shaft taking his weight, and then he was standing on her deck streaming wet, unhurried, a big man in a coat that had been expensive before the sea got hold of it. The hook had a forged head on it as long as Wren's forearm, made for dragging wet line in over a gunwale, and he used it for exactly that.

The *Marrow*'s mooring line ran from her bow cleat to an iron ring in the tower at the waterline. He hooked it, walked it in hand over hand, and took two turns and a hitch around his own barge's bitt without looking down, the way Mara had found the crank.

Two boats, one line, one tower. Nothing steering the barge. Nothing driving it. The whole weight of the squall behind it.

"There," he said. "Now nobody has to guess."

Then his voice came down the shaft, thin and all at once, the way a chimney takes smoke.

"Captain Ferreira. The woman in the sling."

Sol's shape at the spoke-box didn't move.

"You've been watching a lamp in that ward five months. So have I. That's a body, not a story, and bodies have owners. Give me her and the *Marrow* and I'll put your two children through the low gate myself before the bell shuts — my hand on the book, Quill can write it down, she can't help herself. Children safe on the high ground. What you lose is a hollowed woman you never met and a boat you can't keep anyway." He set the hook's shaft on the deck and leaned on it. "You gave up twelve thousand for two children. I watched you do it and I still don't believe it, because it doesn't behave like a price. So I'm offering you the same thing twice. Out loud, captain. I'll wait. I'm the only thing out here tonight that isn't sinking."

Wren looked down. The water in the shaft had come up over the footboard. Mara stood in it to the ankle, counting under her breath, fourteen, fifteen, in the voice of a woman telling strangers where the aspirin lives.

Her copper was cut and taped to the wall a hand's width from itself. She had no line to that boat, none, not one word. She had a chimney and her lungs.

She put the bolt-cutters between her teeth and started up.

Six rungs took her legs out of the water's reach. The cold stayed in them anyway, the way it does.

Through the hatch came Rusk's voice, unhurried, laying the berths out again like a man reading a menu to somebody who had already ordered. Under it Dey, high and cracking, telling him what he could do with his berths and where. Then the drum changed its note.

A winch holding a load knocks. A winch losing one screams. The *Marrow*'s did neither. What came down the shaft instead was a hiss, long and soft, the sound rope makes going out under load with nothing on the brake but its own weight.

She went up the last of it fast and came out at the shaft head, across the coaming on her belly, over the fender, over the rail, into rain that hit like grit off a shovel.

The winch's brake quadrant was open. The quadrant was the half-ring of notched iron the brake shoe bit down into, and the pin was the steel peg that dropped through it to lock the whole thing dead. The peg was gone. In its place Rusk had a marlinspike — a foot of tapered iron, the tool you open the lay of a rope with so it will take a splice — and he set the point against the drum flange and drove it with the heel of his hand. Once. Twice. On the third it stood up out of the iron with the wet line jammed under it, and the hiss stopped.

"There," he said. "Now it isn't a machine. It's a rope with a spike in it. Machines have owners. Ropes have hands, and hands cost."

The load went off the brake and into that spike, and Wren watched the flange take it, and thought about how long a spike stands when the load is a woman in a sling and the ebb is pulling her seaward from underneath.

Sol had not moved off the spoke-box. Both pots knocking, rain off the peak of her cap, one hand flat on the throttle quadrant.

"Third time," she said. "No. And stop reading me, Rusk. I'm not a page."

"It doesn't behave like a price," Rusk said, almost kindly. "Nothing you've done tonight behaves like a price. A thing that isn't a price is a bluff, and a bluff is a thing I can call. I've called worse on less."

"Then call it with your hands full."

Wren got to the winch and did the last thing she would get to do with a free hand. She pulled the slate out of her inside pocket, out of the rain, and woke the screen with her thumb.

Her eleven seconds sat struck through. *Front. Served.* Nothing of hers left in the brass for the bell to take, nothing left in her to be billed for. Under it, in her own hand from an hour ago: *copper cut. ends taped.* No live line off this tower, none, not one word running down into that ward from up here. Whatever the Caller was eating tonight, it was not going to be fed off the *Marrow*.

She put the slate away and it was the first thing she'd closed out all night, and there was no time to feel anything about it.

The tail was going.

Four fathom of free line off the drum, the length you leave long so a man can take a turn on a bitt without stopping the load — the bitt being the pair of iron posts on the deck you tie to — and it was snaking for the scupper with the ebb's pull on it. The lay had opened where the sheave at the shaft head had been chewing: the strands standing up in a fuzz, three of them, and one going by her hand with a crack like a knuckle.

She got a boot on it. Then both fists.

It came bar-tight and it did not stop coming, and she went down on one knee on the deck plate with the line running hot through her palms, and there was nobody topside to say no to any of it. Sol had said her no. It had been for Rusk.

Rusk turned with the boat hook, saw what she had, understood it half a second ahead of her, and started across the deck.

Up the shaft, unhurried, pleasant as weather: "Seventeen."

"Bayo," Wren said. "Both hands. Now."

Bayo left the wheel spinning. With the dead barge shouldered into the Marrow’s quarter and the mooring line taking every pound of steerageway, the wheel was a spoke with nothing to say to the water. He left it spinning and crossed the deck to the bitt—the pair of iron posts set just abaft the mast, the things you heave a line around when you want the boat to stop moving and start holding.

The tail of the ascent line was snaking across the wet plate toward the scupper, the ebbing water pulling it seaward strand by strand. The sheave at the shaft head had been chewing it: the lay had opened, three strands standing up in a fuzz like a cat’s back, one of them already cracked through.

Bayo got his shoulder to the iron, took a turn, then another, and dropped to one knee on the deck plate. He clapped the tail between both palms and held.

It bit.

Not the clean grab of a new rope on dry iron. This line had been underwater fourteen months, and the salt had rotted the heart while the outside still looked sound. The friction came up fast, hot enough to steam the rain off his palms before it started cooking the skin underneath. He felt it go red, then white, then the flat numb that doesn’t warn you before it takes.

Fourteen months ago he’d cut this same line clean. Salas’s line. Salas down in the air pocket at forty-two meters, the marlinspike driven through the rope, the voice in the dark going quiet because Bayo had said he’d hold and then hadn’t. He’d never said it out loud. Some things you can’t unsay once the water’s got them.

Now the line was his again, and it remembered.

"Sol!" he shouted. The rain ate half of it. He cupped his mouth and shouted again, louder, his throat going raw. "Gap’s to port! Starboard of the drowned spire, two fathom left of the leaning tower! Take it now!"

Sol couldn’t leave the spoke-box. Both pots were knocking, one hand flat on the throttle quadrant, her whole body turned to reading the water off the cork floats. If she left the helm to come forward, the Marrow would swing broadside into the tower and the lift-frame would take Mara with it.

Bayo couldn’t leave the bitt. If he let go to grab the wheel, Mara went into the shaft and the marlinspike Rusk had driven in the drum would take the whole load on one bent iron tooth. If he released the tail, the line ran free and the barge had them all.

So he held, and he shouted, and the line cooked his palms while the tower counted up the shaft.

Rusk came across the deck toward him, boat hook in hand, unhurried. "Let it go, pilot," Rusk called over the rain. "She’s mine."

Bayo didn’t look at him. He couldn’t. His eyes were on Sol’s cap at the spoke-box, on the rain running down her face, on the gap ahead where the water stood black and still between two drowned street grids. He shouted the gap a third time.

The line slipped a finger’s breadth. Heat bloomed in his right palm, sharp as a pot handle. He tightened his left. The bitt iron cut into his shoulder. He held.

Behind him the wheel span free, nobody at it, the Marrow drifting toward the gap with the squall at her back and Rusk’s dead barge shoved into her side. The ascent line was the only thing keeping her from crushing the frame against the tower steel and taking Mara straight down the shaft.

A strand parted with a snap like a knuckle, and the line jerked in Bayo’s left hand. He caught it, and the hot rope took the skin off his palm in one clean strip. He smelled it—burnt hair and grease—and his eyes watered. He shouted the gap again, and he didn’t let go.

Rusk was three paces away now, the forged head of the hook glinting gray in the rain, close enough that Bayo could see the stain on his coat where the salt had eaten the wool.

"If you won’t take a price," Rusk said, "I’ll take the line."

Bayo’s palms were going numb. He couldn’t feel the tail anymore except as pressure, a thick cord cutting into the meat below his thumb. One more strand and it would part clean. One more part and the weight would come on the marlinspike in the drum, and a foot of tapered iron was not built to hold a woman in a sling against the ebb.

"Sol!" he shouted. "Take the gap now or never!"

The boat shuddered. Sol had put her to it. The Marrow came off her fenders and jumped, a sound like a crate dropped off a shoulder, and the line went bar-tight in Bayo’s hands. The bitt groaned. The second strand began to smoke.

Rusk raised the boat hook. The ash shaft came level with Bayo’s ribs.

Bayo held on, his hands ruined, his voice gone, and the gap closing ahead of them like a door. He could feel the line beginning to give in his left hand, one fiber at a time, and he knew with the cold certainty of a man who had already cut one line and lived with it that he was about to cut another—only this time the cut would be the sea’s, not his.
